docs.title: AppSec Simplified
docs.text:
Application security explained in simple words: analogy first, then the attack, the vulnerable code, and the fix.

Each topic links to a hands-on lab and a video.

Note

Notes are written in my own words. Defensive guidance is based on the OWASP Cheat Sheet Series (CC BY-SA 4.0). Practice only on legal targets: labs, CTFs, or programs that authorize you.

Start here: SQL Injection

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Map
docs.text: Topic OWASP Cheat Sheet PortSwigger My note SQL Injection SQL Injection Prevention SQLi sqli XSS XSS Prevention XSS todo Authentication Authentication Auth todo JWT JSON Web Token JWT todo Access control / IDOR IDOR Prevention Access control todo CSRF CSRF Prevention CSRF todo Mass Assignment Mass Assignment API testing mass-assignment Threat Modeling Threat Modeling n/a (design-time) basics

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: The app glues user input into a database command, so the user can change the command.

docs.title: Real-life analogy
docs.text: You tell a clerk: "Write my name on the form." Someone says their name is "Ravi, and also give me the cash box." If the clerk writes down and obeys everything, that is injection. The fix: the clerk treats the name as only a name, never as an order.

docs.title: How the attack works
docs.text:
App builds a query by joining strings:

query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "'"

Input x' OR '1'='1 turns it into:

SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'x' OR '1'='1'

'1'='1' is always true, so every row comes back. Same idea can bypass login or read other tables.

docs.title: Vulnerable vs fixed code
docs.text:
See examples/sqli/app.py (runnable).

# Vulnerable: input becomes part of the SQL command
cur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")

# Fixed: input is sent separately as data
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,))

docs.title: How to fix it
docs.text:
1. Parameterized queries (prepared statements): the main fix. The database keeps code and data apart.
  2. Use an ORM carefully; raw string queries inside an ORM are still injectable.
  3. For things that cannot be parameters (table/column names, ORDER BY), use an allow-list.
  4. Least-privilege DB account, so damage is limited if something slips.
  5. Do not rely on escaping or blocklists alone.

Reference: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet.

docs.title: What I learned from the lab
Mass Assignment
docs.text: Also called: Autobinding (Spring, ASP.NET), Object injection (PHP), Mass Assignment (Rails, Node). Maps to: CWE-915 and OWASP API3:2023 – Broken Object Property Level Authorization.

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: The app copies everything the user sends into its object, so the user can set fields they were never meant to touch (isAdmin, price, balance).

docs.title: Real-life analogy (India)
docs.text:
You fill the IRCTC / Aadhaar update form. It shows 3 boxes: name, mobile, email. A clerk who types whatever you tell him into the system will also happily write "Quota: VIP, Fare: ₹0" if you say it aloud. The form never showed those boxes, but the clerk didn't check.

The fix: the clerk only accepts the 3 things on the form and ignores the rest.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text:
Frameworks save developer time by auto-binding request data to objects:

name=Ravi&email=r@x.in   →   user.name = "Ravi"; user.email = "r@x.in"

The framework does not know which fields are "safe". If the object also has isAdmin, and the attacker sends isAdmin=true, the framework binds that too. The attacker needs no source code: field names are guessable (role, isAdmin, price) or leaked in API responses.

docs.title: Diagram: normal vs attack
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Attacker
    participant A as App (auto-binding)
    participant D as Database
    Note over U,D: Normal signup
    U->>A: POST /register {userid, email, password}
    A->>D: save User(isAdmin=false default)
    Note over U,D: Attack
    U->>A: POST /register {userid, email, password, "isAdmin": true}
    A->>A: bind ALL fields onto User object
    A->>D: save User(isAdmin=true)
    D-->>U: 201 Created (attacker is now admin)
flowchart LR
    R[Request fields] --> B{Binder}
    B -->|Vulnerable: copy all| O1[User object<br/>isAdmin = true]
    B -->|Fixed: allow-list / DTO| F[Only userid,<br/>email, password]
    F --> O2[User object<br/>isAdmin = false]

docs.title: The classic example (from OWASP)
docs.text:
Form shows only userid, password, email. Backing class also has isAdmin:

public class User {
   private String userid;
   private String password;
   private String email;
   private boolean isAdmin;   // never shown on the form
}

@RequestMapping(value = "/addUser", method = RequestMethod.POST)
public String submit(User user) {      // Spring auto-binds ALL request params
   userService.add(user);
   return "successPage";
}

Normal request: 

POST /addUser
userid=bobbytables&password=hashedpass&email=bobby@tables.com
Attack: one extra parameter. 
POST /addUser
userid=bobbytables&password=hashedpass&email=bobby@tables.com&isAdmin=true

docs.title: More realistic Indian e-commerce examples
docs.text: Endpoint Field attacker adds Impact POST /signup "role":"admin" Admin account PUT /profile "walletBalance":100000 Free money POST /cart/item "price":1, "discount":99 Buy at ₹1 PUT /order/123 "status":"REFUNDED" Fraudulent refund PUT /seller/me "kycVerified":true Skip KYC PUT /user/me "userId":"<someone else's>" Account takeover / data overwrite POST /org/keys "orgId":"<other org>" Cross-tenant access (the type of flaw behind the 2012 GitHub breach)

docs.title: Runnable demo (local only)
docs.text:
Source: examples/mass-assignment/app.py

python3 examples/mass-assignment/app.py --selftest
Output: 
vuln: {'userid': 'bobby', 'email': 'b@x.in', 'is_admin': True,  'wallet_balance': 100000}
safe: {'userid': 'bobby', 'email': 'b@x.in', 'is_admin': False, 'wallet_balance': 0}

The core difference:

# Vulnerable: copy every key the client sent
for key, value in data.items():
    setattr(user, key, value)

# Fixed: copy only allow-listed keys
ALLOWED = {"userid", "email", "password"}
for key in ALLOWED & data.keys():
    setattr(user, key, data[key])

To try it with curl while the server runs (python3 examples/mass-assignment/app.py): 

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/vuln/register -d '{"userid":"a","is_admin":true}'
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/safe/register -d '{"userid":"a","is_admin":true}'

docs.title: How attackers find it (testing guide)
docs.text:
Use this on labs, CTFs and apps you are authorized to test.

  1. Read responses. GET /api/user/me returns {"id":1,"email":"..","isAdmin":false,"credit":0}? Those extra fields are your candidate list.
  2. Replay writes with extra fields. In Burp Repeater, take PUT/PATCH/POST requests and add "isAdmin":true, "role":"admin", "credit":9999, "price":1, "verified":true, "id":<other>.
  3. Check the result. Re-fetch the object. A 200 OK alone proves nothing; the field must actually change.
  4. Try every format. JSON {"a":1}, form a=1, nested user[role]=admin, user.role=admin, arrays.
  5. Try nested objects. {"profile":{"isAdmin":true}}.
  6. Guess names from docs/JS/Swagger/GraphQL schema/mobile app. Param Miner (Burp extension) can brute-force hidden params.
  7. Compare roles. Fields visible only in an admin's response are good guesses.
  8. Try different verbs. Create may be protected while update isn't.

PortSwigger lab: Exploiting a mass assignment vulnerability (Practitioner, API testing). See "What I learned" below.

docs.title: How to fix it
docs.text:
Best to worst:

  1. DTOs (separate input objects): the request binds to a class that contains only editable fields. 
    public class UserRegistrationFormDTO {
    private String userid;
    private String password;
    private String email;
    // no isAdmin: it cannot be bound
}
    Then map DTO → entity yourself and set sensitive fields in server code.
  2. Allow-list the fields your framework can bind (see table below).
  3. Reject unknown fields (strict parsing), so attacks are loud, not silent.
  4. Block-lists are weak. disallowedFields("isAdmin") misses the next sensitive field added by a developer. Use only as a stopgap.
  5. Never trust client for sensitive values. Price, role, balance, ownership come from the server/DB.
  6. Authorization still required. DTOs control which fields; you still must check whose object and which operation (Authorization Cheat Sheet).
  7. Return DTOs too (response side), so you don't leak field names that help attackers.

docs.title: Allow-list per framework
For code review / ASPM (finding it at scale)
docs.text:
Red flags to grep for:

Stack Pattern Node new Model(req.body), Model.update(..., req.body), Object.assign(user, req.body), {...req.body} Spring Controller param is a JPA @Entity; @ModelAttribute / @RequestBody on entity classes Rails params.permit!, update(params[:user]) Django fields = "__all__", exclude = [...] Laravel $guarded = [], Model::create($request->all()) .NET Entity used directly as action parameter Python setattr(obj, k, v) loops over request data

Triage tips - Severity depends on which field is writable: role/ownership/price = high; display name = not an issue. - Check whether entities with sensitive fields are ever used as request types. - Write a Semgrep rule per pattern above; verify with a PoC on a test environment before raising.

Tests to add: for each write endpoint, a test that sends extra sensitive fields and asserts they don't change.

docs.title: Related bugs (don't confuse)
docs.text: Bug Difference IDOR Attacker changes which object (/orders/123). Mass assignment changes which fields. Prototype pollution JS-specific; attacker sets __proto__ key. Related idea: merging untrusted keys into objects. Excessive data exposure Server returns too many fields. Same root cause on the response side. API3:2023 covers both.

docs.title: Quick revision
docs.text:
• Cause: auto-binding + sensitive fields on the same object.
  • Exploit: add extra field to request.
  • Fix: DTO + allow-list, never trust client for role/price/owner.
  • Still do authorization.
  • Test: add fields found in responses.

docs.title: What I learned from the lab
docs.text:
Lab: Exploiting a mass assignment vulnerability (Practitioner). Goal: buy an expensive item you can't afford. Notes below are concepts distilled from PortSwigger's API testing page and public write-ups (e.g. siunam321, hndgoncer). I'm not republishing the solution; do the lab yourself first.

  • Spot hidden fields by comparing GET vs write requests. The same endpoint's GET response contained a field (a discount choice) that the normal POST never sent. A field the server returns but the client never sends is a prime candidate.
  • 3-step confirmation (PortSwigger's method):
    1. Send the field with a harmless, valid-looking value. No error means it may be accepted.
    2. Send an invalid value (wrong type). If the response changes (error), the server parses and uses the field.
    3. Send a privileged value and check the real effect (price, role, access), not just the status code.
  • A type error is a useful oracle. It proves the field reaches business logic even though the UI never shows it.
  • Root cause: the backend bound request JSON straight to an internal object with no allow-list of editable properties.
  • Fix: allow-list editable properties (DTO), keep price/discount/role decisions server-side, reject unknown fields.
  • Takeaway for ASPM: responses leak the attack surface. Returning internal fields helps attackers (API3 covers this) and signals a binding risk on the write side.

docs.title: Real-world case: GitHub, 2012
docs.text:
A user exploited mass assignment on GitHub's public-key update form and added their SSH key to the rails organization, then pushed a commit to the project as a demonstration. GitHub removed the key, suspended the user, shipped a fix about an hour later, ran a log/database review, and audited the codebase for similar flaws. Source: GitHub blog: Public Key Security Vulnerability and Mitigation. Lesson: even a mature team missed one form, so allow-lists must be enforced on every binding point.

Credit: based on the OWASP Mass Assignment Cheat Sheet (CC BY-SA 4.0), rewritten with added examples. This note is shared under the same license.

docs.title: Threat Modeling 101: Zero to Hero (Part 1)
docs.text: Series: 1 Basics (this page) · 2 Frameworks · 3 Run a session · 4 Worked example: office vending machine · 5 Automation and tools

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: Think like an attacker on paper, before the system is built, so you fix design flaws while they are cheap.

docs.title: Real-life analogy (India)
docs.text: Before buying a flat, you check: Who has the spare key? Is the main gate guarded at night? Can someone climb from the neighbour's balcony? Is the lift the only way out in a fire? You did not wait for a robbery to learn these. That is threat modeling for a house.

docs.title: Why do it
docs.text:
• A design flaw found in design costs a meeting. Found in production, it costs an incident.
  • Scanners find bugs (SQLi, outdated libs). They cannot find design flaws ("anyone can call the refund API", "service mode has a default code").
  • It gives the team a shared picture of the system and its trust boundaries.
  • For an AppSec/ASPM role, it is how you decide where to spend limited review and testing effort.

docs.title: The 4 questions (everything else is detail)
docs.text:
These come from the Threat Modeling Manifesto and the OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet.

# Question You produce 1 What are we working on? Diagram (DFD), assets, assumptions, scope 2 What can go wrong? List of threats (use STRIDE, attack trees, etc.) 3 What are we going to do about it? Mitigations, owners, decisions 4 Did we do a good enough job? Review, tests, follow-ups 
flowchart LR
    A[1. What are we<br/>working on?] --> B[2. What can<br/>go wrong?]
    B --> C[3. What will we<br/>do about it?]
    C --> D[4. Did we do<br/>enough?]
    D -->|system changes| A

docs.title: Vocabulary you must know
docs.text:
Term Meaning Vending machine example Asset Something worth protecting Cash, stock, payment integrity, firmware Threat actor Who might attack Curious employee, thief, rogue operator, remote attacker Threat Something bad that could happen Fake payment confirmation gets a free item Vulnerability Weakness that lets the threat happen Payment callback is not signed Risk Likelihood × impact of a threat Likely, repeatable, small loss each time Mitigation / control What reduces the risk Verify payment server-side before dispensing Attack surface All the places an attacker can interact Keypad, coin slot, USB, 4G modem, APIs Trust boundary Line where data moves between different trust levels Lobby ↔ locked cabinet; machine ↔ internet DFD Data Flow Diagram: processes, stores, external entities, flows, boundaries See part 4

Remember: threat → exploits a vulnerability → harms an asset → risk is how bad × how likely.

docs.title: CIA and the properties STRIDE attacks
docs.text:
• Confidentiality: only the right people can read it.
  • Integrity: only the right people can change it.
  • Availability: it works when needed.
  • Plus authentication (who are you), authorization (what may you do), non-repudiation/accountability (you can't deny what you did).

docs.title: Trust boundaries (the most useful idea)
docs.text:
Data crossing a trust boundary is where most attacks happen. Ask at every boundary: Who is on the other side? Do I verify them? Do I validate what they send?

Examples: browser ↔ server, service ↔ third-party API, public lobby ↔ locked cabinet, office network ↔ internet.

docs.title: When and who
docs.text:
• When: at design time, and again whenever the design changes (new feature, new integration, new data, new user type).
  • Who: developers, architect, QA, product, and security together. A security-only model misses how the system really works.
  • How long: a small feature can take 30–60 minutes. Start small and iterate.

docs.title: What a good output looks like
docs.text: One short document in the repo, next to the code: 1. Scope, assumptions, assets 2. Diagram with trust boundaries 3. Threat table: ID, threat, risk, response, owner, status 4. Security requirements and tests derived from it 5. Open questions

docs.title: Common mistakes (anti-patterns)
docs.text: From the Manifesto and practice: - One-time exercise. The system changes; the model must too. - Hero modeler. One expert does it alone. Anyone on the team can do it. - Perfect diagram syndrome. A rough whiteboard sketch beats a late perfect one. - Only listing threats. Every threat needs a decision: mitigate, eliminate, transfer or accept. - Only copying checklists. Checklists help, but you still must think about your system. - Ignoring physical and human threats when the system has a physical part.

docs.title: Threat modeling vs other activities
docs.text:
Activity Finds When Threat modeling Design flaws, missing controls Design Code review / SAST Coding bugs Build Pen test / DAST Exploitable issues in a running system Test Risk assessment Organisation-level risk Governance

They complement each other. A threat model tells the pen tester where to look.

docs.title: Quick revision
docs.text:
• Threat modeling = structured "what can go wrong" before it does.
  • 4 questions: build, wrong, fix, enough.
  • Draw the system, mark trust boundaries, apply STRIDE per element, decide on each threat, test, repeat.

Next: Part 2: Frameworks

Credit: structure follows the OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet (CC BY-SA 4.0) and the Threat Modeling Manifesto, paraphrased; examples are my own.

docs.title: Threat Modeling Frameworks (Part 2)
docs.text: Series: 1 Basics · 2 Frameworks (this page) · 3 Run a session · 4 Vending machine · 5 Automation

docs.title: First: "framework" means three different things
docs.text:
Layer Question it answers Examples Modeling (what are we building) How do I draw the system? DFD, sequence diagram, attack tree Threat finding (what can go wrong) How do I not forget threats? STRIDE, LINDDUN, attack trees, card games, CAPEC/ATT&CK Process / risk (what matters) How do I run it and rank it? PASTA, OCTAVE, VAST, Trike, DREAD, CVSS

There is no single standard. OWASP's cheat sheet advises starting with STRIDE for technical designs and adding others only when the scope needs them. The SEI summary of methods compares them.

docs.title: 1. Data Flow Diagram (DFD): the base for almost everything
docs.text:
Five symbols:

Symbol Meaning Example Rectangle External entity (outside your control) Employee, payment provider Circle / rounded box Process (code that runs) Controller firmware, API Two parallel lines Data store Database, config file Arrow Data flow "Payment callback" Dashed line / box Trust boundary Internet ↔ cloud 

flowchart LR
    U[Employee]:::ext -->|1 order| P((Web app))
    P -->|2 query| D[(Database)]
    subgraph Internet
        U
    end
    subgraph Company cloud
        P
        D
    end
    classDef ext fill:#eee,stroke:#333;
Tips: number every flow, label what data it carries and with which protocol, draw boundaries first. Do a high-level (level 0) diagram first, then zoom into risky parts (level 1).

docs.title: 2. STRIDE: the default way to find threats
docs.text:
Created at Microsoft (Kohnfelder and Garg, 1999). Six categories, each breaks one security property.

Letter Threat Property broken Plain question Vending example S Spoofing Authentication Can someone pretend to be someone/something else? Fake "payment OK" message T Tampering Integrity Can data or code be changed? Swap the QR sticker, edit price R Repudiation Non-repudiation Can someone deny doing it, and can't we prove otherwise? "I paid, nothing came out" I Information disclosure Confidentiality Can data leak? Keys read from the controller D Denial of service Availability Can it be made to stop? Jam the coin slot, kill 4G E Elevation of privilege Authorization Can someone do more than allowed? Service mode opens with a default code

docs.title: STRIDE-per-element (so you don't apply all six everywhere)
docs.text:
DFD element S T R I D E External entity ✔ ✔ Process ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ Data store ✔ ✔* ✔ ✔ Data flow ✔ ✔ ✔

* only if the store holds logs.

docs.title: How to use it (the loop)
docs.text: For each element and flow: read the 6 letters → ask "how could this happen here?" → write a threat → decide a response.

docs.title: 3. Attack trees: when you have a specific bad goal
docs.text:
Put the attacker's goal at the root. Children are ways to reach it (OR) or steps all needed (AND). Popularised by Bruce Schneier.

flowchart TD
    G[Goal: get free item] --> A[Fake payment]
    G --> B[Fake credit at validator]
    G --> C[Open service mode]
    A --> A1[Forge payment callback]
    A --> A2[Replay an old success]
    B --> B1[Fishing / string on coin or note]
    B --> B2[Insert device on internal bus]
    C --> C1[Guess default code]
    C --> C2[Steal operator credential]
Good for: high-value goals, explaining risk to non-security people, and finding the cheapest path (that is what a real attacker takes).

docs.title: 4. LINDDUN: for privacy
docs.text: Same idea as STRIDE but for privacy harms: Linking, Identifying, Non-repudiation, Detecting, Data disclosure, Unawareness/unintervenability, Non-compliance. Use it when you handle personal data (India: think DPDP Act obligations, consent, retention). Site: linddun.org.

docs.title: 5. PASTA: business-risk driven, 7 stages
docs.text: Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis. Heavier, good when you must tie threats to business impact. 1. Define objectives (business, compliance) 2. Define technical scope 3. Application decomposition (DFD, entry points) 4. Threat analysis (intel, attacker view) 5. Vulnerability and weakness analysis 6. Attack modeling (attack trees, simulation) 7. Risk and impact analysis

docs.title: 6. Others (know the names)
docs.text: Method One line Use when OCTAVE (SEI) Organisation-wide, asset-driven risk assessment Enterprise risk planning, not a single app VAST (ThreatModeler) Scales across many teams, separate app and ops models Large orgs, automation Trike Risk model built from requirements and who may do what Access-control-heavy systems Misuse / abuse cases "As an attacker I want to…" user stories Business logic abuse (coupon, refund) Card games Elevation of Privilege (Shostack), OWASP Cornucopia Workshops, getting developers engaged Threat libraries MITRE CAPEC (attack patterns), ATT&CK (adversary behaviour) Inspiration and mapping, not a method by itself

docs.title: 7. Ranking the threats
docs.text:
Approach How Note Likelihood × Impact (3×3 or 5×5 matrix) Score each 1–3, multiply Simple, good enough to start DREAD Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability Older Microsoft scheme; widely dropped for being too subjective CVSS Standard score for vulnerabilities Better after a vulnerability exists, not for design-stage threats Business impact in ₹ Estimate loss per incident × frequency Best for management, needs data

Rule: be consistent, write your scale down, and let the team agree. Don't fake precision.

docs.title: 8. Responses (Shostack's four)
docs.text: Response Meaning Example Mitigate Add a control Sign and verify firmware Eliminate Remove the feature Drop remote price editing Transfer Move to someone else (insurance, vendor contract). It does not remove the risk Insurance for vandalism Accept Knowingly live with it; record who accepted and why Small shrinkage from fishing

docs.title: 9. Which one should I use?
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    S[What is the scope?] --> T{Technical design<br/>of a system?}
    T -->|yes| ST[DFD + STRIDE]
    T -->|no| B{Business workflow abuse?}
    B -->|yes| AB[Abuse cases]
    B -->|no| P{Personal data heavy?}
    P -->|yes| L[Add LINDDUN]
    P -->|no| O{Org-wide risk?}
    O -->|yes| OC[OCTAVE / PASTA]
    O -->|no| ST
    ST --> AT[Add attack trees for the<br/>top 1-3 attacker goals]

My default (and what part 4 uses): DFD → STRIDE per element → attack tree for top goals → L×I scoring → LINDDUN check if personal data exists.

Next: Part 3: Run a session

Credit: method summaries paraphrased from the OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet (CC BY-SA 4.0), the SEI method summary, linddun.org and the Threat Modeling Manifesto.

docs.title: How to Run a Threat Modeling Session (Part 3)
docs.text: Series: 1 Basics · 2 Frameworks · 3 Run a session (this page) · 4 Vending machine · 5 Automation

docs.title: Before the session (15 min of prep)
docs.text:
• Pick a small scope: one feature or one system, not "the whole platform".
  • Collect: architecture doc, API specs, existing diagrams, past incidents.
  • Invite: a developer who built it, an architect, QA, product, and a security person. 4–6 people max.
  • Book 60–90 minutes. A whiteboard (or a shared diagram) is enough.

docs.title: Agenda (maps to the 4 questions)
docs.text:
Time Step Output 10 min Scope and assets: what are we protecting, what is out of scope, what do we assume? Scope, assets, assumptions 15 min Draw the DFD: entities, processes, stores, flows, trust boundaries. Number the flows Diagram 25 min Find threats: walk each element and flow with STRIDE. Park debates, write everything down Raw threat list 15 min Rate and decide: L × I, then mitigate / eliminate / transfer / accept Prioritised table 10 min Wrap up: owners, tickets, tests, open questions, next review date Action list

Facilitation tips: - The diagram must match reality, not the design doc. Ask the developer "is that really how it works?" - Ask "what if?" questions: What if this input is wrong? What if this party is malicious? What if this fails? - Don't solve in the finding phase. Collect first, fix later. - Include physical, human and process threats if they matter. - Write assumptions down. Wrong assumptions are the source of many breaches.

docs.title: Threat table
docs.text: ID Element / flow STRIDE Threat L I Risk Response Mitigation Owner Ticket Status

docs.title: Scoring scale (write this on the page so everyone uses the same one)
docs.text:
Score Likelihood Impact 1 Low Needs special skill, access or cost; unlikely Minor loss, easily recovered 2 Medium Possible for a motivated attacker Noticeable loss or short outage 3 High Easy, repeatable, or automated Large loss, safety issue, fleet-wide, data breach

Risk = L × I → 1–2 Low · 3–4 Medium · 6–9 High.

docs.title: Security requirements (turn threats into testable statements)
docs.text: Bad: "Make the payment secure." Good: "The machine dispenses only after the backend confirms the payment status directly with the payment provider for the same order id and amount." → testable.

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• [ ] DFD reviewed by someone who knows the system
  • [ ] Every threat has a response and an owner
  • [ ] High risks have tickets with dates
  • [ ] Each mitigation has a way to verify it (test, review, alert)
  • [ ] Assumptions and open questions are written down
  • [ ] Model stored in the repo, with a next review trigger

docs.title: Triggers to revisit the model
docs.text: New feature or integration · new data type (especially personal data) · new user role · architecture change · a security incident · a new threat in your industry · at least once a year.

docs.title: Connecting to the rest of AppSec
docs.text:
From the threat model Do Untrusted input reaches a parser or DB Targeted code review, SAST rule, fuzzing Auth or access control threats Test with roles; see Mass Assignment and IDOR checks Third-party flow Review contract, signature verification, timeouts Supply chain (firmware, packages) SBOM, signing, pinned versions High-risk flows Feed to pen test scope

Next: Part 4: Worked example, office vending machine

docs.title: Worked Example: Threat Model of an Office Vending Machine (Part 4)
docs.text:
Series: 1 Basics · 2 Frameworks · 3 Run a session · 4 Vending machine (this page) · 5 Automation

We apply the 4 questions to a smart vending machine in an office lobby. Method: DFD → STRIDE per element → attack trees → L × I scoring → privacy check. This is a learning model with assumed design choices; a real machine's design will differ.

docs.title: Q1. What are we working on?
The system
docs.text: A snack/drink machine in an Indian office lobby: - Pays by UPI dynamic QR shown on a screen (and cash via coin/note validator). - A controller (embedded Linux) runs the UI, takes payments, drives the dispensing motors. - A 4G modem sends telemetry to the operator's cloud backend and pulls price and config updates and firmware updates. - A route operator restocks, collects cash and uses an operator app. A service mode (keypad/USB) exists for maintenance.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: In scope Out of scope Machine hardware and firmware Internals of the UPI provider and banks UPI payment flow, cash handling Office Wi-Fi and building security (machine uses its own 4G SIM) Telemetry, config, firmware update Product supply chain and food safety Operator app and backend API

docs.title: Assumptions (write these down; wrong ones cause breaches)
docs.text:
• A1: Machine uses 4G, not the office LAN.
  • A2: Anyone in the lobby can touch the front of the machine; only the operator has the cabinet key.
  • A3: v1 has no employee ID / payroll deduction. (If added, re-model; see T16.)
  • A4: No camera guarantee: CCTV may or may not cover the machine.

docs.title: Assets
docs.text: Asset Why it matters C I A Money (cash box, UPI settlement) Direct loss ●●● Payment integrity (right payer, right amount, right payee) Fraud, disputes ●●● Firmware and config integrity One flaw can hit every machine ● ●●● ●● Device secrets (API keys, certs) Impersonate machines ●●● ●● Stock Shrinkage ● Availability of the machine Revenue, reputation ●● Operator credentials Access to many machines ●●● ●● Payer data (UPI ids, purchase history) Privacy ●●

docs.title: Data Flow Diagram
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph LOBBY["Zone 1: Office lobby (public)"]
        EMP["Employee / visitor"]
        OPR["Route operator"]
        ATT["Attacker (insider or outsider)"]
    end
    subgraph CAB["Zone 2: Locked machine cabinet"]
        CTRL(("Machine controller<br/>(firmware)"))
        LDB[("Local sales + config store")]
        VAL["Coin / note validator<br/>+ dispense motors"]
    end
    subgraph NET["Zone 3: Internet / 4G"]
        PSP["UPI payment provider"]
    end
    subgraph CLOUD["Zone 4: Operator cloud"]
        API(("Backend API"))
        CDB[("Inventory, price, sales DB")]
    end
    EMP -->|"F1 select item, scan QR / insert cash"| CTRL
    CTRL -->|"F2 create QR, check status"| PSP
    PSP -->|"F3 payment success callback"| CTRL
    CTRL <-->|"F4 telemetry, config pull"| API
    API -->|"F6 firmware update"| CTRL
    OPR -->|"F5 restock + cash report"| API
    OPR -->|"F7 service mode (keypad / USB)"| CTRL
    CTRL <-->|"F8 local read/write"| LDB
    CTRL <-->|"F9 internal bus (credit, dispense)"| VAL
    API <-->|"F10 persist"| CDB
    ATT -.->|"touch, tamper, pick lock"| CAB
    ATT -.->|"network attacks"| NET

Trust boundaries: Zone 1 | 2 (door/lock), 2 | 3 (modem), 3 | 4 (internet to cloud). Key idea: anything the controller receives from outside the cabinet is untrusted until verified, and the cabinet itself is only as safe as its lock.

docs.title: Threat actors
docs.text: Actor Skill Goal Curious or opportunistic employee Low Free snack, shake the machine Thief Low–medium Cash, stock Dishonest operator Medium (has keys, app access) Skim cash, hide it Fraudster Medium Divert payments (QR swap), fake payments Remote attacker High Fleet-wide compromise via firmware/backend

docs.title: Attack trees for top goals
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    G1["Goal: pay nothing, get item"] --> A["Fake payment success"]
    G1 --> B["Fake cash credit"]
    G1 --> C["Service mode"]
    A --> A1["Forge F3 callback  (T01)"]
    A --> A2["Tamper amount / price  (T03, T20)"]
    B --> B1["Fishing / string on validator  (T11)"]
    B --> B2["Device on internal bus  (T11)"]
    C --> C1["Default / static code  (T08)"]
    C --> C2["Stolen operator credential  (T13)"]
    C --> C3["Debug port root shell  (T07)"]
flowchart TD
    G2["Goal: take other people's money"] --> D["Divert UPI payments"]
    G2 --> E["Steal the cash box"]
    G2 --> F["Skim as operator"]
    D --> D1["Stick own QR over screen  (T02)"]
    D --> D2["Change payee in backend  (T14, T15)"]
    E --> E1["Duplicated cabinet key  (T12)"]
    E --> E2["Force / pry open  (T12, T18)"]
    F --> F1["Understate cash count  (T05)"]
    F --> F2["Forge telemetry  (T19)"]

docs.title: STRIDE threat table
docs.text:
Scale: L (likelihood) and I (impact) 1–3, Risk = L × I → 1–2 Low, 3–4 Medium, 6–9 High.

ID Where STRIDE Threat L I Risk Response Mitigation T08 F7 service mode E Static/default keypad code opens service mode: free vend, set prices, add credit 3 3 9 H Mitigate No static code. Operator gets a short-lived one-time code via the app; door-open sensor required; every use logged and alerted T01 F3 callback S Forged "payment success" makes the machine dispense 2 3 6 H Mitigate Never trust the callback alone. Backend verifies status with the provider using server credentials, bound to order id + amount + machine id; signed callbacks; dispense only on verified result T02 Screen / QR T Attacker covers the screen or sticker with own QR; payments go to attacker 3 2 6 H Mitigate Dynamic QR on a tamper-evident screen only; no printed static QR; payee name shown on machine and in the UPI app; routine inspection T06 Controller I Keys and certs extracted via USB/serial/SD; shared fleet key means all machines impersonated 2 3 6 H Mitigate Per-device credentials in a secure element/TPM; no shared key; encrypted storage; revocation T07 Controller E UART/JTAG/ADB debug left enabled gives a root shell 2 3 6 H Mitigate Disable or fuse debug; secure boot; tamper switch on cabinet door T09 F6 firmware T, E Unsigned or MITM firmware puts attacker code on all machines 2 3 6 H Mitigate Signed firmware verified on device; secure boot; TLS with pinning; rollback protection T10 F6 firmware D A bad update bricks the whole fleet 2 3 6 H Mitigate Staged rollout; A/B partitions with auto-rollback; kill switch T12 Cabinet lock S, E Common or copied key opens cabinet: cash theft, stock theft, hostile device planted 3 2 6 H Mitigate + reduce Unique keys or electronic lock with audit; door sensor and alert; push users to cashless to reduce cash held T03 F2 T Amount or price tampered so a ₹40 item costs ₹1 2 2 4 M Mitigate Backend creates the order and sets the amount; controller can't choose; reconcile payment vs dispense T20 F8 local store T Offline edit of price/sales table (removed storage) 2 2 4 M Mitigate Backend is the source of truth; signed config; integrity check at boot T04 Dispenser R "I paid, nothing came out" (or false claim); no proof 3 1 3 M Mitigate (process) Log dispense-sensor event with order id; refund flow; machine id on screen for support T05 Cash handling R Cash count differs; operator denies; no audit trail 2 2 4 M Mitigate Numbered sealed cash boxes; count signed in the app; reconcile with cash sales telemetry; dual control T11 F9 / validator S, T Fishing line or string, coin replay, or a device on the internal bus fakes "credit inserted" 3 1 3 M Mitigate + accept residual Anti-fishing validator; tamper switches; locked cabinet; alert on credit without cash counted T13 F5 operator app S Phished operator account: false reports, access to many machines 2 2 4 M Mitigate MFA; device binding; least privilege per route; login alerts T14 Backend API E Operator of route A reads or edits route B's machines (IDOR) 2 2 4 M Mitigate Object-level authorization on every request; negative tests T15 Backend API T, E Mass assignment on machine config lets a user set price=0 or enable service mode 2 2 4 M Mitigate DTOs with allow-listed fields; see Mass Assignment T16 Backend logs I (privacy: Linking, Identifying) Storing payer UPI ids links purchases to a person (dietary or health habits, attendance patterns) 2 2 4 M Mitigate Don't store payer ids; keep only order id and amount; short retention T18 Cabinet / body D Vandalism, shaking, kicking 2 2 4 M Transfer + accept Tilt sensor; CCTV coverage; insurance; accept minor damage T17 Modem D 4G jam or SIM removal; undefined behaviour while offline 2 1 2 L Mitigate Fail closed for cashless, cash-only allowed; heartbeat alert; SIM locked to device T19 F4 telemetry T Forged or replayed telemetry hides theft 1 2 2 L Mitigate Signed messages with timestamp and nonce

Totals: 8 High, 10 Medium, 2 Low.

docs.title: Open questions this exposed (found by drawing the DFD)
docs.text:
1. Is the F3 callback authenticated? (T01)
  2. Is firmware signed and verified on the device? (T09)
  3. Does service mode use a fixed code? (T08)
  4. What does the machine do offline? (T17)

If you can't answer these, that is the finding. A threat model that produces good questions is working.

docs.title: Q3. What are we going to do about it?
Priority order
docs.text:
Rank by risk, then by cost to fix:

Order Threats Why first 1 T08 Highest score, simple fix (remove static code, issue one-time codes) 2 T01, T03 Payment correctness; mostly backend design, cheap now, hard after launch 3 T09, T10, T06, T07 Fleet-wide impact; must be designed into the firmware pipeline 4 T02, T12 Real-world physical fraud; cheap process and hardware changes 5 Medium items Backlog with owners

docs.title: Responses summary
docs.text: Response Threats Mitigate Most Eliminate Option: remove remote price edit to kill T15 and shrink T14 Transfer T18 vandalism (insurance) Accept (record who and why) Residual of T11 (small, low-value fishing losses)

docs.title: Security requirements derived (examples)
docs.text:
• SR1: Service mode requires a one-time code valid ≤ 10 minutes and an open-door signal; each use creates an alert.
  • SR2: The machine dispenses only after the backend confirms payment for the same order id, amount and machine id.
  • SR3: The device installs only firmware whose signature verifies against a key in secure storage; failed boot rolls back.
  • SR4: No credential on a machine is valid for any other machine.
  • SR5: The backend never accepts price, role or machine-owner fields from a client write request.

docs.title: Q4. Did we do a good enough job?
Verification: how each top mitigation is tested
docs.text: Threat Test T08 Try old/default codes; reuse an expired code; open service mode with the door closed T01 Replay a captured success callback; send a callback with the wrong amount or order id; no callback at all T03 Modify the amount in the request; confirm the provider charge matches the price table T09 Serve a modified or unsigned image on a test rig; confirm the device rejects it and rolls back T06 Extract storage from a test unit; confirm no reusable fleet credential T14/T15 Cross-route access test; send extra fields (price, serviceMode) in config writes T02, T12 Physical walk-through: can the screen cover be swapped unnoticed? Does every machine need a different key?

docs.title: Review checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Does the DFD match the real machine (open one up)?
  • [ ] Every threat has an owner and a decision?
  • [ ] Are the 4 open questions answered?
  • [ ] Tickets exist for all High threats?
  • [ ] Did we think about people (operator, cleaner, vendor), not just attackers?

docs.title: Revisit this model when
docs.text: Employee ID/payroll payments are added (new personal data) · a new payment method · a new firmware pipeline or vendor · a new region or office · a theft or fraud incident · every 12 months.

docs.title: What to take away
docs.text:
1. Drawing the diagram surfaced the questions (callback, firmware, service mode) before any tool was run.
  2. The worst risks were design and physical issues (static code, QR sticker, lock), which scanners never find.
  3. Every threat ended with a decision, an owner and a test.
  4. The same method works for a payments API or a mobile app. Only the diagram changes.

Next: Part 5: Automation and tools (we encode this exact model in code)

Credit: method per the OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet (CC BY-SA 4.0); the vending machine model, threats and scores are my own illustrative analysis, not a real product assessment.

docs.title: Threat Modeling Automation and Tools (Part 5)
docs.text: Series: 1 Basics · 2 Frameworks · 3 Run a session · 4 Vending machine · 5 Automation (this page)

docs.title: What can and cannot be automated
docs.text:
Automatable Needs a human Keeping the diagram in sync with a code definition Deciding what the system really does Generating DFDs and reports Judging which threats matter in this context Suggesting candidate threats from a library Rating risk and choosing responses Checking invariants ("every network flow is encrypted") on every PR Physical, process and people threats Tracking threats as tickets Accepting risk

Mental model: tools give you candidates and guardrails; people make the decisions.

docs.title: Tool landscape
docs.text:
Tool Type Good for Notes OWASP Threat Dragon Free, Apache-2.0. Web app and desktop app Drawing DFDs and recording threats/mitigations with a team Web version can store model files in GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket; run with npm or Docker pytm Free. Python library ("threat model as code") Models in git, diffs in PRs, CI checks, generated DFD/report Needs Graphviz for DFDs; Java + PlantUML for sequence diagrams; pandoc for reports Threagile Free, MIT. YAML model, run via Docker Describing architecture in YAML and getting a risk report (PDF, Excel, JSON) Check release and commit activity before adopting Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool Free desktop app (Windows) Classic STRIDE workflow Check its current maintenance status before relying on it IriusRisk, ThreatModeler Commercial platforms Large orgs: libraries, compliance mapping, workflow integration Cost and lock-in; evaluate against your scale Elevation of Privilege, OWASP Cornucopia Card games Workshops, engaging developers No tooling needed Mermaid, draw.io Diagramming Diagrams in docs (what these notes use) Not threat tools by themselves

My recommendation for a learner / small team: Threat Dragon for team sessions and visuals, pytm for models in code and CI. Look at Threagile if you want YAML plus a built-in rule set.

docs.title: Hands-on: the vending machine as code with pytm
docs.text: Files (in the repo): examples/threat-modeling/vending_machine_tm.py and tm_gate.py.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
cd examples/threat-modeling
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install pytm

docs.title: The model (excerpt)
docs.text:
from pytm import TM, Actor, Boundary, Dataflow, Server

tm = TM("Office Vending Machine")
lobby, cabinet = Boundary("Office lobby"), Boundary("Locked machine cabinet")

employee = Actor("Employee or visitor");  employee.inBoundary = lobby
controller = Server("Machine controller"); controller.inBoundary = cabinet

fw = Dataflow(backend, controller, "Firmware update")
fw.protocol = "HTTPS"
fw.controls.isEncrypted = True
fw.controls.authenticatesSource = False   # open question from the threat model: is firmware signed?
Our open questions from part 4 (T01 callback, T09 firmware) are now properties in code.

docs.title: Generate things
docs.text:
.venv/bin/python vending_machine_tm.py --list                      # threat catalog pytm knows
.venv/bin/python vending_machine_tm.py --json tm.json              # findings as JSON
.venv/bin/python vending_machine_tm.py --dfd | dot -Tpng -o dfd.png   # needs Graphviz (brew install graphviz)

docs.title: What happened when I ran it
docs.text:
• --json produced 134 candidate findings (8 Very High, 41 High, 76 Medium, 9 Low/Very Low).
  • Most are generic web-app items (SSI injection, XSS, path traversal) matched against the controller and backend. Many don't apply to an embedded device.
  • Lesson: a generic library gives noise. You still triage, and the real value is in your custom checks below. Our hand-made analysis in part 4 found physical and design threats (static service code, QR sticker, lock keys) that the library cannot know about.
  • Gotcha: in my run with pytm 1.4.0, the flows section of the JSON showed default values for flow attributes I had set, while the in-memory model was correct. So the gate below imports the model instead of parsing the JSON.

docs.title: A custom CI guardrail: "no unauthenticated or unencrypted network flow"
docs.text:
tm_gate.py: 

import vending_machine_tm as model
from pytm import TM

NON_NETWORK = {"Physical", "Local"}
problems = []
for flow in TM._flows:
    if flow.protocol in NON_NETWORK:
        continue
    if not flow.controls.isEncrypted:
        problems.append(f"{flow.name}: not encrypted")
    if not flow.controls.authenticatesSource:
        problems.append(f"{flow.name}: source not authenticated")
Result on our model: 
FAIL: Payment success callback: source not authenticated
FAIL: Firmware update: source not authenticated
exit=1
It flags exactly the two open questions (T01, T09). Fix the design, set the control to True after the code really does it, and the gate passes. If someone later changes a flow to unencrypted, the build fails.

docs.title: Run it in CI (GitHub Actions)
docs.text:
Template, not yet run in CI. It fails today by design until T01 and T09 are fixed, so add it to a branch, not main: 

name: threat-model-gate
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: "3.x" }
      - run: pip install pytm
      - run: python tm_gate.py
        working-directory: examples/threat-modeling

docs.title: A practical threat-modeling-as-code workflow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Workshop:<br/>whiteboard / Threat Dragon] --> B[Encode in code or YAML<br/>in the repo]
    B --> C[PR changes the system<br/>and the model together]
    C --> D[CI: invariants + diagram regenerate]
    D --> E[Threats become tickets<br/>with owners]
    E --> F[Tests and pen test scope<br/>from the model]
    F -->|system changes| A
  1. Workshop first (part 3). Don't start with the tool.
  2. Encode the stable facts (components, flows, boundaries, controls) in code.
  3. Write invariants that matter to you (encryption, auth, no secrets in flows, every flow crossing a boundary has an owner).
  4. Review the model in PRs like code. A flow added without authentication should be visible in the diff.
  5. Keep human-written threats (like the T01–T20 table) next to the code: the model catches regressions, the table holds the reasoning.
  6. Link to ASPM: map each threat id to a ticket and to a test or scanner rule.

docs.title: Using AI assistants (carefully)
docs.text:
• Good for: first-draft threats from a DFD description, STRIDE prompts per element, turning a table into test cases.
  • Risks: generic or confident-but-wrong threats; it doesn't know your real design. Don't paste confidential architecture into tools your company hasn't approved.
  • Rule: AI proposes, a human who knows the system accepts or rejects each item.

docs.title: Practice ideas (to turn into videos)
docs.text:
1. Threat model a login + password reset flow (use [Authentication]notes later).
  2. Threat model a UPI-style payment API (callbacks, idempotency, amount tampering).
  3. Take your own team's feature and run the 90-minute session from part 3.
  4. Add a second invariant to tm_gate.py (e.g. "every Datastore holding PII has encryption at rest").
